blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: ANOVA (analysis of variance) tests whether three or more group means are equal. It splits the total variability of the outcome into a between-group part and a within-group part and compares them with an F-ratio (recall §5.7.2.5).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: With four clinics there are six pairs. Testing each pair at α = 0.05 inflates the chance of at least one false positive. If the six tests were independent and every H₀ true, that chance would be 1 − 0.95⁶ = 0.265 (recall the complement rule, §5.2.3). ANOVA asks one question instead: is the spread of the group means larger than the spread within groups would produce by chance? One test, one α.

points.html: F = (between-group mean square) ÷ (within-group mean square). Under H₀ both estimate the same variance, so F is near 1.
H₀: all population means are equal. A significant F says at least one differs; it does not say which. §9.5.3 covers comparing specific groups.
Assumptions are those of the t-test (§9.2.4): independence, approximate Normality within groups, equal variances. Welch’s ANOVA relaxes the equal-variance assumption, as Welch’s t-test does.
Forms covered: one-way (§9.5.2), two-way (§9.5.4), repeated measures (§9.5.5).

blocks.html: Logic of ANOVA – Partitioning Variance

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
For k groups with nᵢ observations each (N in total), group means ȳᵢ and grand mean ȳ:

  • SST = Σ(y − ȳ)² (total), df N − 1
  • SSB = Σ nᵢ(ȳᵢ − ȳ)² (between groups), df k − 1
  • SSW = Σ(y − ȳᵢ)² (within groups), df N − k
  • SST = SSB + SSW; MSB = SSB/(k − 1); MSW = SSW/(N − k); F = MSB/MSW with (k − 1, N − k) df.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Each observation’s distance from the grand mean has two parts: its group mean’s distance from the grand mean (signal) plus its own distance from its group mean (noise). Squaring and summing keeps the two parts separate. Dividing each sum by its df turns it into a variance estimate, a “mean square”. MSW estimates the common within-group variance whatever the truth. MSB estimates the same variance only if H₀ is true, and is inflated if the means differ.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
1. y − ȳ = (ȳᵢ − ȳ) + (y − ȳᵢ).
  2. Square and sum over everyone: Σ(y − ȳ)² = Σnᵢ(ȳᵢ − ȳ)² + Σ(y − ȳᵢ)² + 2Σ(ȳᵢ − ȳ)(y − ȳᵢ).
  3. Within group i, (ȳᵢ − ȳ) is constant and Σ(y − ȳᵢ) = 0 (deviations from a mean sum to zero, recall §2.2.1), so the cross term is 0. Hence SST = SSB + SSW exactly.
  4. The df add the same way: (N − 1) = (k − 1) + (N − k).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Birthweights (kg) of five newborns at each of three PHCs:

PHC A PHC B PHC C
2.6, 2.8, 2.9, 3.0, 2.7 3.0, 3.1, 2.9, 3.3, 3.2 2.9, 3.0, 2.8, 3.1, 2.7
mean 2.80 mean 3.10 mean 2.90

blocks.alt: Three-PHC birthweights with group means and grand mean
blocks.caption: Figure 9.2. Each dot is one newborn. Orange bars are the PHC means; the dashed line is the grand mean, 2.933 kg. Arrows show the between-group deviations that make up SSB; the scatter of dots around each orange bar makes up SSW.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Grand mean ȳ = 44.0 ÷ 15 = 2.933 kg.
  2. SSB = 5 × [(2.80 − 2.933)² + (3.10 − 2.933)² + (2.90 − 2.933)²] = 5 × (0.01778 + 0.02778 + 0.00111) = 0.2333.
  3. SSW: within PHC A, deviations −0.2, 0, 0.1, 0.2, −0.1 give 0.10; PHC B and PHC C also give 0.10 each. SSW = 0.300.
  4. SST = 0.2333 + 0.300 = 0.5333 (check: Σ(y − 2.933)² = 0.5333).
  5. ANOVA table:
Source SS df MS F
Between PHCs 0.2333 2 0.1167 4.67
Within PHCs 0.3000 12 0.0250
Total 0.5333 14
  1. The 95% point of F(2, 12) is 3.89. F = 4.67 > 3.89, so reject H₀ at the 5% level; p = 0.032.

points.html: SST = SSB + SSW is an identity, not an approximation; this split is what “analysis of variance” means.
MSB uses k − 1 df, MSW uses N − k. Always report both df with F: here F(2, 12) = 4.67.
The same between-versus-within comparison measures clustering in the intraclass correlation coefficient (§15.2.1: the share of total variance lying between clusters).

blocks.html: One-Way ANOVA

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: One-way ANOVA applies §9.5.1 when the groups are defined by one categorical factor.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: “One-way” means one factor, such as PHC or wealth quintile. With exactly two groups, one-way ANOVA is the pooled t-test: F = t² (recall t²_ν = F(1, ν), §5.7.2.5), and the p-values are identical.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
cl <- read.csv("data/clinic_children.csv")
cl$quintile <- factor(cl$wealth_quintile)
tapply(cl$weight_kg, cl$quintile, mean)
fit <- aov(weight_kg ~ quintile, data = cl)
summary(fit)
       1        2        3        4        5 
11.34615 11.99615 11.99048 12.39000 12.81000 
            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)  
quintile     4  19.41   4.853   2.457 0.0508 .
Residuals   95 187.68   1.976

Mean weight rises from 11.35 kg in the poorest quintile to 12.81 kg in the richest. The table has the layout of §9.5.1: SSB = 19.41 on 5 − 1 = 4 df, SSW = 187.68 on 100 − 5 = 95 df, F = 4.853 ÷ 1.976 = 2.46, p = 0.051. factor() matters: without it, R would treat quintile as a number and fit a straight-line trend instead of five separate means.

points.html: F(k − 1, N − k); report the group means and SDs, not only F and p.
A significant F says the means are not all equal. A non-significant F does not show they are equal (recall §8.5). Here p = 0.051 is weak evidence, not evidence of no difference.
Wealth and weight here are observational: the gradient is an association, not an effect of wealth.

blocks.html: Post-Hoc Tests and Multiple Comparisons

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Multiple comparison procedures test several hypotheses together while controlling an error rate for the whole set. The family-wise error rate (FWER) is the probability of at least one false positive among the k tests. The false discovery rate (FDR) is the expected proportion of false positives among the hypotheses rejected. Post-hoc tests are multiple comparison procedures for pairs of group means after ANOVA.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Every test at α = 0.05 carries a 5% false-positive risk when its H₀ is true, and the risks accumulate. Procedures fall into two families. Bonferroni-type methods adjust p-values or α and work for any set of tests. Methods built for group means, such as Tukey’s and Dunnett’s, use the joint distribution of the comparisons and are more powerful for that job.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
1. Independent tests, all H₀ true (recall the multiplicity note in §8.5): P(no false positive) = (1 − α)ᵏ by the multiplication rule (recall §5.2.2), so FWER = 1 − (1 − α)ᵏ.
  2. Any tests: P(at least one of k events) ≤ the sum of their probabilities (the addition rule without the overlap term, recall §5.2.1). Testing each at α/k gives FWER ≤ k × α/k = α. That is Bonferroni, and it needs no independence.
  3. Holm: sort the p-values p₍₁₎ ≤ … ≤ p₍ₖ₎. Compare p₍₁₎ with α/k, p₍₂₎ with α/(k − 1), and so on; stop at the first non-rejection. It controls the FWER and rejects everything Bonferroni rejects, and sometimes more (Holm, 1979).

blocks.label: Worked Calculation 1: how fast the FWER grows (α = 0.05, independent tests)
blocks.html:
Tests, k FWER = 1 − 0.95ᵏ Bonferroni α/k
3 0.143 0.0167
5 0.226 0.010
6 0.265 0.0083
10 0.401 0.005

blocks.label: Worked Calculation 2: Bonferroni, Holm and BH on four p-values
blocks.html:
A trial reports four secondary outcomes with p = 0.004, 0.015, 0.020 and 0.20.

  1. Bonferroni: multiply by 4: 0.016, 0.060, 0.080, 0.80. One outcome significant.
  2. Holm: compare 0.004 with 0.05/4 = 0.0125 (reject); 0.015 with 0.05/3 = 0.0167 (reject); 0.020 with 0.05/2 = 0.025 (reject); 0.20 with 0.05 (stop). Three significant. Adjusted p-values: 0.016, 0.045, 0.045, 0.20.
  3. Benjamini–Hochberg (BH): compare p₍ᵢ₎ with (i/k) × 0.05 = 0.0125, 0.025, 0.0375, 0.05. The largest i satisfying it is i = 3, so reject the first three. Adjusted p-values: 0.016, 0.027, 0.027, 0.20.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation 3: Tukey’s HSD on the three PHCs (§9.5.1)
blocks.html:
Tukey’s honestly significant difference uses the studentized range distribution: the distribution of (largest − smallest of k sample means) ÷ (their estimated SE) when all true means are equal.

  1. From that distribution, q(0.95; k = 3, df = 12) = 3.773.
  2. HSD = q × √(MSW/n) = 3.773 × √(0.025/5) = 3.773 × 0.0707 = 0.267 kg.
  3. Pairwise differences: B − A = 0.30 (> 0.267, significant); B − C = 0.20; C − A = 0.10 (both < 0.267). Only PHC B differs from PHC A.
  4. For contrast, Fisher’s least significant difference (LSD) is an ordinary pooled t-test for each pair: t₁₂ × √(2 × MSW/n) = 2.179 × 0.1 = 0.218 kg. It makes no correction for the three comparisons.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
cl <- read.csv("data/clinic_children.csv")
cl$quintile <- factor(cl$wealth_quintile)
fit <- aov(weight_kg ~ quintile, data = cl)
TukeyHSD(fit)
p.adjust(c(0.004, 0.015, 0.020, 0.20), method = "holm")
p.adjust(c(0.004, 0.015, 0.020, 0.20), method = "BH")

...

[1] 0.016 0.045 0.045 0.200

All ten pairwise differences of §9.5.2 get intervals with a joint 95% coverage. Only the richest vs poorest quintile (5 − 1) excludes 0: 1.46 kg (0.07 to 2.86), adjusted p = 0.034. This happened although the overall F in §9.5.2 had p = 0.051. There is no contradiction: F spreads its power over every way the five means could differ, while Tukey concentrates on pairs. The p.adjust lines reproduce the Holm and BH columns of Worked Calculation 2.

points.html: A significant F is not a precondition for Tukey, Dunnett, Bonferroni or Holm. These control the FWER on their own. GraphPad’s statistics guide states that “all the multiple comparisons tests offered by Prism are valid even if the overall ANOVA did not find a significant difference among means”, and quotes Maxwell and Delaney: requiring a significant omnibus test first “only serves to lower alpha … below the desired level … and hence inappropriately decreases power”. The F-test gate belongs to Fisher’s LSD, which makes no correction of its own: “protected” LSD is run only after a significant F. The same guide calls protection “no longer recommended” because it controls the FWER poorly.

Tukey vs Dunnett. Tukey compares every pair. Dunnett compares each treatment with one control only, “comparing several treatments simultaneously with a control or standard treatment” while keeping a joint significance level (Dunnett, 1964). It makes fewer comparisons, so it is more powerful for that question: four treatment arms against placebo give 4 comparisons instead of Tukey’s 10.
Bonferroni vs Holm. Holm is uniformly at least as powerful and equally valid, so there is little reason to report plain Bonferroni except for its simplicity.

FDR. In screening many hypotheses (for example, dozens of biomarkers), controlling the FWER is very strict. Benjamini and Hochberg (1995) proposed “controlling the expected proportion of falsely rejected hypotheses — the false discovery rate”. It gives more power when many hypotheses are false, and it suits exploratory screening rather than a trial’s confirmatory outcome.

Planned vs unplanned. A few comparisons specified in the protocol before seeing the data can be tested directly, with a correction for that small number only. Comparisons chosen after looking at the data need a full correction.

Subgroup analyses are multiple comparisons too. Testing an effect in 10 subgroups gives a FWER of 0.40 when there is no effect in any (Worked Calculation 1). An effect “significant in women but not in men” is not evidence that the effect differs by sex; that needs a test of interaction (§9.5.4).

questions.prompt: A one-way ANOVA comparing four clinics is significant. A colleague concludes “all four clinics differ from each other”. What is wrong, and what should be done next?
questions.answer: A significant F says only that the four means are not all equal: at least one differs from at least one other. It could be one clinic differing from the other three. To find which pairs differ, use a multiple comparison procedure: Tukey’s HSD for all six pairs, or Dunnett’s test if each clinic is compared with one reference clinic. Report the pairwise differences with their adjusted CIs. (These procedures do not require the F-test to be significant first.)

questions.prompt: A study tests 8 independent hypotheses at α = 0.05, all nulls true. What is the FWER? What is the Bonferroni per-test α?
questions.answer: FWER = 1 − 0.95⁸ = 1 − 0.663 = 0.337: about a one-in-three chance of at least one false positive. Bonferroni per-test α = 0.05 ÷ 8 = 0.00625.

questions.prompt: A one-way ANOVA has 4 groups and N = 24, with SSB = 6.0 and SSW = 20.0. Complete the ANOVA table and decide at α = 0.05 (the 95% point of F(3, 20) is 3.10).
questions.answer:
Source SS df MS F
Between 6.0 4 − 1 = 3 2.0 2.0
Within 20.0 24 − 4 = 20 1.0
Total 26.0 23

F = 2.0 < 3.10: do not reject H₀ (p = 0.15). The data do not show a difference between the group means; they do not show the means are equal.

blocks.html: Two-Way ANOVA

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Two-way ANOVA tests the effects of two categorical factors on a quantitative outcome at the same time: the main effect of each factor and their interaction, meaning that the effect of one factor depends on the level of the other.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The one-way split of §9.5.1 becomes SST = SS(factor 1) + SS(factor 2) + SS(interaction) + SS(within), each with its own F. The interaction asks something neither one-way analysis can: is the gap between supplemented and unsupplemented mothers the same at every clinic?

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Mean birthweight (kg) by clinic and maternal supplementation (hypothetical):

Clinic No supplementation Supplementation Gain
A 2.80 2.85 0.05
B 2.85 3.30 0.45
C 2.90 3.00 0.10
D 2.75 2.95 0.20

blocks.caption: Figure 9.3. Mean birthweight at four clinics with and without supplementation. Parallel lines would mean no interaction; here the gain ranges from 0.05 kg (clinic A) to 0.45 kg (clinic B).

points.html: Three F-tests: factor 1, factor 2, interaction (df = (a − 1)(b − 1) for factors with a and b levels).
If the interaction is real, a single “effect of supplementation” (here an average gain of 0.20 kg) misdescribes every clinic; report the effect by clinic.

With unequal cell sizes the sums of squares depend on the order of entry; software offers alternatives. Two-way ANOVA is a special case of multiple regression with categorical predictors (Chapter 12), which handles unbalanced designs more transparently.

blocks.html: Repeated Measures ANOVA

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Repeated measures ANOVA (RM-ANOVA) compares the means of the same subjects measured at three or more time points or conditions. It removes between-subject variation from the error term, as the paired t-test does for two measurements (§9.2.3).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Measurements on one person are correlated, so treating time points as independent groups would be wrong. RM-ANOVA treats each subject as a block: a set of related measurements whose shared level is removed before the time points are compared. It adds an assumption, sphericity: the variances of the differences between every pair of time points are equal. When sphericity fails, the Greenhouse–Geisser correction reduces the df to keep the Type I error near α.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Systolic BP in 6 patients at baseline, 1 month and 3 months after starting treatment:

Patient 0 m 1 m 3 m Change per month (3 m − 0 m) ÷ 3
1 152 146 140 −4.0
2 160 158 151 −3.0
3 148 147 145 −1.0
4 156 150 147 −3.0
5 164 160 152 −4.0
6 150 149 147 −1.0

blocks.label: Worked Calculation: the summary-measure approach
blocks.html:
RM-ANOVA asks “do the three time-point means differ?”. The clinical question is usually “how fast does BP fall?”. Matthews, Altman, Campbell and Royston (1990) recommend a two-stage method: reduce each subject’s series to one clinically meaningful number, “such as a rate of change or an area under a curve”, then analyse those numbers “by simple statistical techniques as though they were raw data”.

  1. Stage 1: each patient’s change per month (last column).
  2. Stage 2: mean = −2.67 mmHg/month, SD = 1.37, SE = 1.37/√6 = 0.558.
  3. One-sample t-test against 0 (§9.2.1): t = −2.67 ÷ 0.558 = −4.78, 5 df, p = 0.005. 95% CI: −2.67 ± 2.571 × 0.558 = −4.10 to −1.23 mmHg/month.

Using all three visits to fit a straight line for each patient gives a better slope; that uses regression (Chapter 12).

points.html: RM-ANOVA generalises the paired t-test, as one-way ANOVA generalises the independent t-test.

Limits. RM-ANOVA needs every subject measured at the same fixed times. A subject with one missed visit is dropped entirely, which wastes data and can bias the result if drop-outs differ from completers. It cannot use unequally spaced or subject-specific visit times, and its F-test answers a vague question (“do the means differ anywhere?”).

Alternatives. The summary-measure approach above is simple and valid (Matthews et al., 1990). Linear mixed models (§15.2.4: regression models with a random intercept or slope for each person) use every available measurement and allow unequal timing, so they suit longitudinal data with missing visits.

questions.prompt: Using the table in §9.5.4, compute the supplementation gain at clinic A and at clinic B, and the difference between the two gains. What does a non-zero difference of this kind represent?
questions.answer: Gain at A = 2.85 − 2.80 = 0.05 kg. Gain at B = 3.30 − 2.85 = 0.45 kg. Difference of gains = 0.45 − 0.05 = 0.40 kg. A difference between the effect of one factor at different levels of the other is an interaction: the benefit of supplementation depends on the clinic. Neither main effect can show this, because each averages over the other factor.

questions.prompt: Haemoglobin is measured in 40 pregnant women at 0, 2 and 4 months; 9 miss the 4-month visit. What does RM-ANOVA do with those 9 women, and name two better approaches.
questions.answer: RM-ANOVA needs complete data, so it drops the 9 women entirely, including their 0- and 2-month values. That loses 22.5% of the sample (9 of 40) and can bias the result if the women who missed the visit differ (for example, sicker or poorer). Better: (a) a summary-measure approach, such as each woman’s change per month computed from the visits she attended, analysed with a one-sample or two-sample t-test (Matthews et al., 1990); (b) a linear mixed model (§15.2.4), which uses every available measurement and allows unequal timing.

questions.prompt: Four children’s weights gain 0.20, 0.30, 0.10 and 0.20 kg per month. Using the summary-measure approach, compute the mean gain and its SE.
questions.answer: Mean = 0.80 ÷ 4 = 0.20 kg/month. Deviations 0, 0.10, −0.10, 0; SD = √(0.02 ÷ 3) = 0.0816 kg/month. SE = 0.0816 ÷ √4 = 0.041 kg/month. (A one-sample t-test against 0 would give t = 4.9 on 3 df.)
